parakeet: A lot of believers have been taught that once they say the word God, the thinking is over. But that word is doing a lot of work that it cannot actually carry. Religious belief often survives by submitting a name for an explanation. And one of the deeper problems is that when people lose confidence in one superstition, they often don't learn how to think more rigorously. They just swap vocabularies. They replace one borrowed name with another borrowed name. What used to be God's plan becomes the universe. What used to be spiritual warfare becomes energy. What used to be calling becomes alignment. The label changes, but the habit stays the same. The process is not deepened. The tools for knowing have not improved, and people still do not know the thing. They just have a new name for what they never learned how to examine. I did an exercise with my children once. I pointed at a rug in the house and asked them, What's that? And like most of us would, they answered with the name, a rug, a carpet. And I told them, No, that's what we call it. That's not what it is. Because naming a thing is not the same thing as understanding a thing. A label is not knowledge. A word is not an explanation. I recently listened to Richard Feynman describe a similar lesson from his childhood. He said that when he was young, he and his father would go walking in the woods, and if he pointed to a bird and asked what it was, his father might give him the name, but then immediately pushes him further. Do you know anything about that bird now that you know the name? Do you know how it lives, how it moves, how it eats, how it survives. The lesson was simple but profound. Knowing the name of a thing is not the same thing as knowing the thing itself.
